points.description: States the correct answer: exactly the positive integers r work.
Verifies that every positive integer r works: A(kr)=0 (2kr is an integer), so B(n,r)=0 and n(n+1)r is a multiple of n.

Shows that a non-integer rational r fails: with r=p/q in lowest terms, q≥2, finds some n (e.g., a multiple of q or suitable n) where n(n+1)r - B(n,r) is not a multiple of n, using the structure of fractional parts of 2kr.

levels.says: Sets up the rational case with r=p/q and computes or analyzes B(n,r) partially, but does not reach a valid contradiction.

points.description: Shows that an irrational r fails (e.g., the condition forces B(n,r) to be such that n(n+1)r - B(n,r) is an integer for all n, hence r is rational, a contradiction), with a valid argument.

levels.says: Has the right idea for irrational r (the expression must be an integer, so r is rational), but with gaps.

rubric.notes: Full marks: answer is all positive integers, with verification that integers work and proofs that non-integer rationals and irrationals fail. Part marks for verification of integers, or for partial progress in the rational/irrational cases. Equivalent methods are accepted. A correct answer with no justification earns only the P1 mark.
